title: Recent Developments in Inertial and Centrifugal Microfluidic Systems and the Governing Forces for Cancer Cell Separation: A Survey Outline

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Microfluidic Cancer Cell Separation
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical significance of cancer cell isolation
subsections.content:
Isolation of cancer cells from patient-derived samples is clinically important because these cells provide a minimally invasive window into disease burden, dissemination, and therapeutic response. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) have been detected in the blood of patients with metastatic carcinomas and, in seminal clinical studies, higher CTC counts were associated with shorter progression-free and overall survival in metastatic breast, prostate, and colorectal cancer, supporting their value as prognostic biomarkers ref [1], ref [2]. Beyond enumeration, recovery of intact viable cells enables downstream molecular analysis that can complement or, in some settings, reduce reliance on repeated tissue biopsy.

The clinical significance of cancer cell isolation extends from prognosis to treatment selection and disease monitoring. Molecular characterization of isolated tumor cells can reveal actionable alterations, epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, and emerging resistance mechanisms that may not be captured by single-site tissue sampling. For example, CTC analyses have been used to interrogate HER2 status discordance in breast cancer and androgen receptor signaling in prostate cancer, illustrating how liquid-biopsy-derived cells can inform biologically relevant heterogeneity over time ref [3], ref [4]. In parallel, circulating tumor DNA and CTC studies together have reinforced the broader concept that serial blood-based sampling can track tumor evolution during therapy ref [5].

These clinical motivations place stringent demands on separation technologies. Cancer cells are typically rare events among vast backgrounds of hematologic cells, and clinically useful platforms must therefore enrich targets with high sensitivity while preserving morphology, viability, and molecular integrity. This need is especially acute because antigen expression can be variable or lost during epithelial-mesenchymal transition, limiting purely marker-dependent capture strategies and motivating label-free approaches that exploit biophysical differences for broader and less biased recovery ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Microfluidic Cancer Cell Separation
subsections.subsection_title: Biophysical basis of cancer cell separability
subsections.content:
Cancer cell separability in microfluidic systems arises from measurable differences in physical phenotype relative to hematologic cells and, in some cases, to normal epithelial counterparts. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are often larger than leukocytes, but size alone is insufficient because their distributions overlap substantially and vary across tumor type, epithelial–mesenchymal state, and treatment history ref [7], ref [6]. This heterogeneity is clinically important: CTC populations include both rigid epithelial-like cells and more deformable, invasive phenotypes, so any label-free separator effectively interrogates a multidimensional biophysical space rather than a single marker.

Key discriminating parameters include cell diameter, shape, deformability, nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, membrane tension, and viscoelastic response. Early mechanical phenotyping showed that malignant transformation and metastatic potential can be associated with reduced stiffness and altered cytoskeletal organization ref [8], while single-cell deformability studies demonstrated that mechanical compliance can distinguish malignant from benign or less aggressive cells ref [9]. In blood, these traits interact with hydrodynamic forces: larger or less deformable cells experience different lift, drag, and shear-induced migration than smaller, highly deformable blood cells, enabling passive fractionation in confined flows.

These biophysical contrasts motivate inertial and centrifugal microfluidics. Inertial devices exploit size- and deformability-dependent equilibrium focusing under finite Reynolds number conditions, whereas centrifugal systems couple density, size, and sedimentation behavior to radial transport. Because CTCs can be rare and phenotypically diverse, successful platforms must preserve viability while accommodating broad distributions in size and mechanical state ref [10], ref [11]. The challenge is therefore not merely to isolate the "largest" cells, but to design operating windows that remain robust to biologically meaningful heterogeneity ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Microfluidic Cancer Cell Separation
subsections.content:
Microfluidic cancer cell separation strategies can be broadly grouped into affinity-based and label-free approaches. Affinity devices exploit antibodies or aptamers against epithelial or tumor-associated markers, exemplified by EpCAM-dependent capture in the CTC-Chip and related geometries, which offer high specificity but may under-recover cells that have undergone epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition or exhibit phenotypic heterogeneity ref [13], ref [14]. This limitation has motivated increasing emphasis on physical-property-based sorting that does not require prior molecular labeling.

Label-free microfluidic methods separate cells according to size, deformability, density, dielectric properties, or hydrodynamic behavior. Deterministic lateral displacement uses pillar arrays to impose size-dependent trajectories, while filtration and constriction-based systems exploit geometric exclusion but remain vulnerable to clogging in clinically relevant samples ref [15]. Active methods, including dielectrophoresis and acoustophoresis, can enrich rare tumor cells through differences in electrical polarizability or acoustic contrast, often with good tunability but at the cost of added instrumentation and tighter operating windows ref [16], ref [17].

Hydrodynamic strategies are especially attractive for processing blood-scale volumes because they can operate continuously with simple device architectures. Inertial microfluidics leverages lift-force and secondary-flow effects for high-throughput focusing and fractionation, and has been translated to rare-cell enrichment in spiral and related channels ref [18]. Centrifugal and other rotation-assisted platforms similarly exploit body-force-driven transport and are well suited to integrated, sample-to-answer workflows. Within the broader microfluidic landscape, these passive or quasi-passive modalities are therefore positioned as practical compromises between throughput, purity, device simplicity, and preservation of cell viability.

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Microfluidic Cancer Cell Separation
subsections.subsection_title: Advantages and limitations of inertial and centrifugal platforms
subsections.content:
Inertial microfluidic platforms are attractive for cancer cell separation because they exploit lift-force and Dean-flow effects to focus particles continuously at high volumetric throughput without external fields or affinity labels. This makes them comparatively simple to operate, readily parallelizable, and compatible with processing clinically relevant blood volumes, as illustrated by spiral and contraction–expansion designs for rare-cell enrichment ref [19], ref [20]. Their label-free operation is particularly valuable when downstream molecular profiling or culture requires preservation of native cell states.

However, inertial separation is fundamentally indirect: performance depends on size, deformability, and hydrodynamic interactions rather than tumor-specific identity. Because circulating tumor cells overlap biophysically with leukocyte subpopulations and can exhibit marked phenotypic heterogeneity, purity and recovery often trade off against each other, and optimization can be sample-specific. In addition, elevated hematocrit, cell aggregates, and non-Newtonian sample properties can perturb equilibrium focusing and reduce robustness in whole-blood operation ref [21], ref [22].

Centrifugal microfluidic platforms offer complementary advantages. By using rotation-driven sedimentation and pressure generation on disc-based devices, they can integrate sample loading, plasma extraction, and cell concentration in sealed, low-dead-volume formats with minimal peripheral hardware, supporting point-of-care deployment ref [23], ref [24]. Yet centrifugal systems typically provide coarser selectivity than finely tuned inertial devices, and prolonged or excessive centrifugal stress may affect fragile cells. More broadly, both classes remain challenged by standardization, recovery of very small or highly deformable tumor cells, and seamless coupling to downstream single-cell analyses ref [24], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Physical Principles and Governing Forces in Inertial and Centrifugal Microfluidics
subsections.content:
Inertial lift forces arise in finite-Reynolds-number microchannel flows when suspended particles disturb the surrounding shear field and interact hydrodynamically with nearby walls. The resulting lateral migration reflects the balance between a shear-gradient-induced lift that typically drives particles away from the channel center and a wall-induced lift that repels them from the boundaries, yielding discrete equilibrium positions in straight channels ref [26], ref [27]. This mechanism underpins label-free focusing because the net lift scales strongly with particle size, commonly approximated as proportional to a^4, making inertial migration especially effective for separating larger circulating tumor cells from smaller blood cells.

The modern microfluidic formulation of inertial focusing was established through experiments showing spontaneous particle ordering and focusing in straight and curvilinear channels at moderate channel Reynolds number ref [28], ref [29]. Subsequent theoretical and numerical work clarified that equilibrium location depends on channel aspect ratio, confinement ratio, and Reynolds number, with rectangular channels often producing face-centered focusing while square channels can support multiple stable positions ref [27], ref [30]. For deformable biological cells, additional complexity arises because cell shape, viscoelasticity, and nucleus-to-cytoplasm structure perturb the rigid-particle scaling and may shift equilibrium streams or broaden focused bands.

For cancer cell isolation, these features are advantageous because inertial lift can enrich rare, larger, and mechanically distinct cells at high volumetric throughput without external fields. However, predictive design requires coupling lift scaling with polydispersity, deformability, and hematocrit-dependent interactions, as emphasized in studies that extended inertial microfluidics from single-particle theory toward practical bioseparation regimes ref [29], ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Physical Principles and Governing Forces in Inertial and Centrifugal Microfluidics
subsections.subsection_title: Dean drag and secondary flow effects
subsections.content:
In curved microchannels, centrifugal acceleration acting on the faster axial core generates a pair of counter-rotating transverse vortices known as Dean flow. The resulting cross-stream Dean drag competes with inertial lift, displacing particles across streamlines and altering equilibrium positions relative to straight channels. This secondary motion is commonly parameterized by the Dean number, De = Re(Dh/2Rc)^1/2, which increases with channel Reynolds number and decreases with radius of curvature, thereby linking geometry directly to transverse mixing and migration strength ref [32], ref [29].

For finite-size particles and cells, the balance between Dean drag and inertial lift determines whether trajectories are focused, bifurcated, or continuously recirculated. In spiral devices, this competition enables size-dependent ordering because larger particles experience stronger lift scaling, whereas smaller particles are more readily entrained by Dean vortices and remain closer to vortex streamlines ref [33], ref [34]. This mechanism underpins high-throughput sheathless separations in curved and spiral channels and has been exploited for rare-cell enrichment, including circulating tumor cell isolation, where subtle differences in size and deformability can shift crossover conditions between lift-dominated and Dean-dominated transport ref [34], ref [35].

Secondary-flow effects are also sensitive to cross-sectional shape. Rectangular and trapezoidal spirals redistribute axial velocity maxima and vortex centers, modifying accessible focusing bands and often improving particle resolution by separating stable equilibrium positions near inner or outer walls ref [35], ref [36]. More broadly, Dean-coupled inertial microfluidics illustrates that separation performance cannot be inferred from Reynolds number alone; it emerges from coupled channel curvature, aspect ratio, particle confinement, and cell mechanical properties ref [29], ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Physical Principles and Governing Forces in Inertial and Centrifugal Microfluidics
subsections.content:
In rotating microfluidic systems, particles and cells experience an outward body force proportional to density contrast, radial position, and the square of angular velocity. In the rotating frame, this centrifugal term provides the primary driving mechanism for sedimentation, band formation, and radial migration, and is commonly exploited in lab-on-a-disc platforms for blood fractionation and rare-cell enrichment ref [37], ref [38]. For a suspended object of volume Vp, the effective radial force scales as (rho_p-rho_f)VpΩ^2r, so even modest density differences can become operationally significant at high rotation rates. This makes centrifugal microfluidics particularly attractive for cancer cell isolation when density-based discrimination is combined with size or deformability effects.

Coriolis forces arise from the relative motion of the particle or fluid within the rotating frame and act perpendicular to the local velocity, scaling as 2mΩ×u. Although usually secondary to centrifugal forcing, Coriolis effects can deflect streamlines, skew particle trajectories, and modify residence times, especially in curved or radially directed microchannels where through-flow coexists with platform rotation ref [39], ref [40]. These effects become important when the Rossby number is small enough for rotation to compete with inertial transport, and they can couple with channel geometry to generate asymmetric focusing or lateral displacement.

For cell-separation design, the key implication is that centrifugal and Coriolis forces rarely act in isolation: they superimpose with viscous drag, lift, and sedimentation-hindered interactions to determine capture efficiency and purity. Reviews and modeling studies of centrifugal microfluidics therefore emphasize balancing rotational speed, channel depth, radial path length, and flow resistance to tune whether cells remain entrained, sediment onto structured regions, or undergo controlled cross-stream migration ref [38], ref [23], ref [41]. In cancer applications, this balance is especially delicate because tumor cells overlap hematologic cells in density, so rotational forcing is most effective when integrated with complementary hydrodynamic selectivity.

subsections.section_title: Physical Principles and Governing Forces in Inertial and Centrifugal Microfluidics
subsections.content:
In inertial and centrifugal microfluidics, viscous drag sets the baseline translational response of suspended cells and particles to the carrier flow, while buoyancy and gravity introduce body-force-driven slip whenever particle and fluid densities differ. For small particle Reynolds number, the drag is well approximated by the Stokes relation, with corrections required as confinement, finite Reynolds number, or wall proximity increase ref [42], ref [43]. In practice, these forces are often secondary to inertial lift in pressure-driven focusing devices, but they become important when flow velocities are modest, residence times are long, or cell density and size distributions are broad.

Gravity-driven sedimentation and buoyancy can bias particle trajectories across channel height, altering the equilibrium positions predicted from lift-only theories and modifying separation fidelity in horizontal and vertically oriented devices. Their importance is commonly expressed through a sedimentation velocity or through dimensionless ratios comparing settling to advective transport; even weak settling can become significant for rare-cell isolation because cancer cells, leukocytes, and debris differ only subtly in density and deformability ref [44], ref [45]. Classical analyses of particle migration in Poiseuille flow also show that gravitational orientation and wall interactions can perturb lateral migration and residence near channel boundaries ref [46].

Under rotation, the apparent body force is amplified by centrifugal acceleration, so buoyancy is replaced by a density-contrast-dependent centrifugal term that scales with radial position. This principle underlies centrifugal sedimentation and density-based plasma or cell fractionation on lab-on-a-disc platforms, where drag balances outward body forces to determine migration speed and pelleting thresholds ref [37], ref [47]. Accordingly, accurate prediction of cancer-cell transport in rotational systems requires simultaneous accounting of drag, effective buoyancy, and inertial cross-stream forces rather than treating these mechanisms independently.

subsections.section_title: Physical Principles and Governing Forces in Inertial and Centrifugal Microfluidics
subsections.subsection_title: Interfacial and capillary forces in rotational platforms
subsections.content:
In rotational microfluidic platforms, interfacial and capillary forces govern liquid positioning, valving, and phase stability in ways that strongly influence particle and cell trajectories. At the microscale, Laplace pressure across curved menisci can oppose or delay centrifugal pumping until a critical rotational speed is reached, enabling passive capillary burst valves and siphon-based routing strategies ref [48], ref [37]. These mechanisms are especially important in disc-based bioanalysis, where abrupt release of trapped liquid can redefine local shear, residence time, and exposure of rare cells to downstream inertial or centrifugal fields ref [49].

Capillary effects are further coupled to wettability, channel geometry, and contact-angle hysteresis, so the threshold for meniscus motion is not determined by centrifugal acceleration alone. Detailed analyses of centrifugal step emulsification and droplet generation have shown that interfacial tension sets breakup conditions and stabilizes discrete compartments against coalescence during spinning ref [50], ref [51]. Such compartmentalization is relevant to cancer diagnostics because droplet encapsulation and phase partitioning can protect fragile cells, isolate secreted biomarkers, or localize immunoassays within rotating cartridges.

A broader design implication is that rotational systems often operate in a regime where body forces scale with fluid density and angular velocity, whereas capillary forces scale with surface tension and inverse curvature. This competition, commonly expressed through Bond- or capillary-type balances adapted for centrifugal fields, determines whether liquids remain pinned, burst across geometric constrictions, or fragment into droplets ref [37], ref [52]. Consequently, control of surface chemistry and interface geometry is as important as control of rotation speed for robust cell isolation workflows on lab-on-a-disc platforms ref [49], ref [52].

subsections.section_title: Physical Principles and Governing Forces in Inertial and Centrifugal Microfluidics
subsections.content:
Dimensionless analysis is central to comparing inertial and centrifugal microfluidic devices across channel geometries, flow rates, and rotational speeds. In pressure-driven inertial focusing, the particle Reynolds number Re_p = Re(a/D_h)^2 usefully scales the onset and strength of lateral migration, linking finite-size effects to the classical channel Reynolds number Re [1,2]. For curved channels, the Dean number De = Re(D_h/2R_c)^{1/2} captures the intensity of secondary vortices and the competition between Dean drag and inertial lift, thereby organizing regimes of focusing, equilibrium-shift, and size-selective separation [3,4].

Rotational systems introduce an additional hierarchy of nondimensional groups. The Rossby number Ro compares axial inertia to Coriolis effects, while the Froude number Fr or, equivalently, ratios built from \omega^2r/g, quantify centrifugal forcing relative to gravity; these become especially important when radial migration and sedimentation act together on rare cancer cells. For suspended particles or cells, Stokes number and density ratio further determine lag relative to fluid streamlines, whereas confinement ratio a/D_h governs how strongly wall-induced and shear-gradient lift scale with size [1,5].

At the platform level, capillary and wetting constraints are often summarized through the Bond number Bo and capillary number Ca, which delimit valving, burst, and interface stability in spinning discs [6]. Such scaling laws are valuable because they collapse seemingly device-specific observations into transferable design rules: inertial enrichment generally requires moderate Re with sufficiently large a/D_h, whereas centrifugal fractionation benefits from high \omega^2r combined with controlled Ro, De, and Bo to preserve predictable trajectories and stable phase boundaries [3,6,7].

subsections.section_title: Inertial Microfluidic Platforms for Cancer Cell Separation
subsections.content:
Straight-channel inertial focusing devices provide the simplest inertial architecture for label-free cancer cell enrichment. In finite-Reynolds-number laminar flow, particles experience a balance of shear-gradient and wall-induced lift forces that drive them toward a limited set of equilibrium positions, with focusing strength increasing strongly with particle size. Foundational studies in rectangular and high-aspect-ratio channels established the scaling laws and equilibrium structures that underpin later cell-separation devices, showing that larger objects migrate more rapidly and can be resolved from smaller blood cells without external fields [1,2].

For cancer applications, straight channels are attractive because they are easy to parallelize and can process dilute or pre-enriched blood samples at relatively high throughput. In practice, separation is achieved by choosing channel dimensions and flow rates so that larger circulating tumor cells (CTCs) focus into distinct lateral streamlines while most leukocytes remain broadly distributed. This design logic was demonstrated in microfluidic systems for continuous size-based enrichment of tumor cells from blood, including inertial focusing strategies that coupled straight-channel ordering with downstream collection [3,4]. Such devices benefit from operational simplicity, but performance can deteriorate when CTCs overlap in size with activated leukocytes or when hematocrit-induced cell-cell interactions disrupt ideal focusing behavior.

A key limitation of straight inertial channels is therefore their dependence on size as the dominant discriminant. Studies of particle and cell migration in rectangular geometries have shown that equilibrium position is also sensitive to confinement, Reynolds number, and particle deformability, implying that biomechanical heterogeneity among tumor cells can broaden focused streams and reduce purity [2,5]. Nonetheless, because they offer predictable force fields, straightforward fabrication, and compatibility with multiplexing, straight-channel devices remain an important baseline platform and are often integrated upstream of more selective inertial or affinity-based stages for CTC isolation [4,6].

subsections.section_title: Inertial Microfluidic Platforms for Cancer Cell Separation
subsections.content:
Spiral microchannels are among the most widely adopted inertial platforms for label-free cancer cell enrichment because curvature-induced Dean vortices act together with inertial lift to generate size-dependent equilibrium positions at high throughput. In these devices, larger and less deformable cells experience stronger net lift and typically focus near the inner wall, whereas smaller blood cells are displaced by Dean drag across streamlines; this enables continuous separation from whole blood or lysed samples without affinity labels. Foundational studies established the underlying Dean-coupled inertial ordering in curved channels and demonstrated efficient particle sorting over broad flow-rate windows, creating the basis for later circulating tumor cell (CTC) applications ref [64], ref [34].

For cancer diagnostics, spiral designs became especially important after high-throughput CTC enrichment from blood was demonstrated using slanted and trapezoidal spiral geometries, which sharpen Dean-flow asymmetry and improve the spacing between cell focusing bands. Warkiani and co-workers reported rapid viable CTC isolation from patient blood in a spiral microfluidic biochip, while subsequent trapezoidal-channel implementations further improved recovery and purity by shifting particle equilibrium positions across the channel height ref [65], ref [66]. These devices are attractive because they combine milliliter-per-minute processing with simple sheathless operation and compatibility with downstream molecular analysis.

Nevertheless, spiral performance is sensitive to the overlap between tumor-cell size distributions and leukocyte populations, as well as to deformability differences that can weaken purely size-based discrimination. Parallelization and optimization of cross-sectional geometry have therefore been pursued to preserve focusing at clinically relevant throughputs and across heterogeneous CTC phenotypes ref [67], ref [68]. More broadly, spiral microchannels illustrate the central trade-off in inertial cancer cell separation: very high throughput and gentle continuous processing, but only partial selectivity when target cells are small, deformable, or phenotypically diverse ref [65], ref [68].

subsections.section_title: Inertial Microfluidic Platforms for Cancer Cell Separation
subsections.content:
Serpentine and other curvilinear inertial microchannels extend the principle of Dean-coupled migration beyond simple spirals by repeatedly reorienting the centrifugal field. Alternating bends generate transverse Dean vortices whose direction changes from turn to turn, while inertial lift continues to drive particles toward size-dependent equilibrium positions. This periodic competition can sharpen focusing, reduce the required channel footprint, and improve robustness over a broader range of flow rates than straight channels alone, especially when channel dimensions are tuned so that larger cells migrate across streamlines more rapidly than smaller blood cells ref [69], ref [29].

For cancer cell isolation, these geometries are attractive because repeated curvature-induced perturbation enhances discrimination among rare, relatively large circulating tumor cells and abundant leukocytes. Di Carlo and co-workers showed that curved and asymmetric channels can exploit size-dependent inertial ordering for high-throughput particle and cell handling, while later studies in sinusoidal and wavy channels demonstrated that curvature modulation can intensify transverse migration and narrow focused bands ref [70], ref [71], ref [72]. In practice, serpentine layouts are often integrated upstream of collection bifurcations or cascaded with other inertial modules to pre-focus suspensions before fractionation.

A key consideration in cancer applications is that curvilinear designs do not rely purely on nominal diameter: Dean drag, wall effects, and repeated acceleration/deceleration can amplify differences in deformability and shape. This is relevant because many tumor cells are larger yet mechanically heterogeneous, so optimal operation typically requires balancing Reynolds and Dean numbers to avoid overlap with activated or enlarged leukocyte subpopulations. Reviews of inertial microfluidics have therefore highlighted serpentine architectures as compact platforms for combining high throughput with tunable biomechanical sensitivity, although their performance remains sample-dependent in whole blood and other clinically complex matrices ref [29], ref [73].

subsections.section_title: Inertial Microfluidic Platforms for Cancer Cell Separation
subsections.content:
Contraction-expansion arrays (CEAs) and obstacle-assisted inertial devices extend size-based focusing beyond simple equilibrium positioning by imposing repeated accelerations, extensional flow, and local streamline curvature. In these geometries, sudden contractions amplify shear-gradient lift, while downstream expansions and recirculation zones perturb trajectories in a size- and deformability-dependent manner, enabling differential lateral displacement of rare tumor cells from smaller blood cells. Early microfluidic filtration studies using deterministic pillar arrays established the utility of obstacle-mediated hydrodynamics for continuous rare-cell isolation, although many operated outside the inertial regime [1]. Subsequent CEA implementations showed that periodic contractions can be used for sheathless, high-throughput particle and cell ordering with tunable cutoffs [2,3].

For cancer applications, these platforms are attractive because they couple inertial effects with cell mechanical response. Unlike straight or spiral channels, obstacles and contraction units can locally enhance stress exposure, making trajectories sensitive not only to diameter but also to deformability and recovery time. This is relevant for circulating tumor cells (CTCs), whose broader size and stiffness distributions often overlap with leukocytes. Studies of inertial sorting in expansion-contraction and pillar-containing channels have shown improved discrimination when repeated perturbation-and-relaxation cycles are used, particularly at high Reynolds number where secondary flows and particle-wall interactions become appreciable [3,4].

Nevertheless, obstacle-assisted designs also face practical tradeoffs. Closely spaced posts or narrow throats increase pressure drop and clogging risk in whole blood, and highly heterogeneous CTC phenotypes can reduce purity if design thresholds are too aggressive. Hybrid architectures that combine obstacle arrays with downstream inertial focusing or Dean-based polishing stages have therefore been explored to balance throughput, recovery, and robustness [4,5,6]. Overall, CEAs and related obstacle-assisted devices offer a useful complement to spiral and serpentine systems when enhanced sensitivity to subtle biomechanical differences is desired.

subsections.section_title: Inertial Microfluidic Platforms for Cancer Cell Separation
subsections.content:
Multi-stage and cascaded inertial systems extend the throughput and selectivity of single-stage devices by sequencing distinct hydrodynamic operations—typically pre-alignment, coarse depletion, and final enrichment—within one workflow. This architecture is especially attractive for circulating tumor cell (CTC) isolation, where extremely rare target cells must be recovered from a vast excess of leukocytes and erythrocytes. Early demonstrations of high-throughput inertial ordering in parallelized channels established the practical basis for such staged processing, showing that inertial focusing can be scaled while maintaining controlled particle positioning at clinically relevant flow rates ref [80].

In cancer-cell applications, cascaded implementations often combine serial Dean-flow sorting modules or repeated inertial filtration steps to progressively sharpen size-based discrimination and improve purity. Hou and co-workers integrated slanted spiral microchannels with downstream membrane filtration for label-free CTC enrichment, illustrating how inertial prefractionation can reduce filter loading and improve overall recovery ref [81]. Warkiani et al. subsequently developed the slanted spiral platform as a high-throughput enrichment method for CTCs from blood, a design logic that readily supports serial or multiplexed operation for enhanced depletion of hematologic backgrounds ref [65].

More broadly, cascaded inertial concepts have been reinforced by sheathless differential focusing strategies and by multiplexed microchannel arrays that increase volumetric throughput without abandoning deterministic particle ordering ref [82], ref [83]. For rare-cell isolation, the principal advantage of multi-stage layouts is that each stage can be tuned to a narrower operating window, partially compensating for overlap in cancer-cell and leukocyte size distributions. However, cumulative residence time, stage-to-stage dispersion, and deformation-dependent trajectory shifts can still limit purity when tumor cells are small or mechanically compliant, motivating hybrid staged systems that combine inertial pre-enrichment with complementary downstream selection mechanisms ref [81], ref [84].

subsections.section_title: Inertial Microfluidic Platforms for Cancer Cell Separation
subsections.subsection_title: Influence of cell deformability and heterogeneity
subsections.content:
Although inertial microfluidic separation is often introduced as a size-based process, cancer-cell behavior in finite-Reynolds-number flows is also strongly modulated by deformability and population heterogeneity. Deformable cells experience altered lift-force balances, shape-dependent rotation, and wall interactions, which can shift equilibrium positions relative to stiffer blood cells even at comparable nominal diameters. This coupling between mechanics and lateral migration was established in early inertial studies of particles and capsules and later extended to cell sorting, showing that apparent focusing fidelity degrades when target populations span broad distributions of size, stiffness, and morphology ref [85], ref [70].

For circulating tumor cells (CTCs), this issue is particularly important because epithelial, mesenchymal, apoptotic, and therapy-altered subpopulations can differ markedly in cortical tension and cytoskeletal organization. Label-free approaches exploiting these differences have shown that deformability itself can be a discriminating biophysical marker: suspended microchannel resonator measurements revealed wide variation in mass and stiffness across tumor cells ref [86], while deformability cytometry studies demonstrated that malignant transformation and metastatic competence are often associated with increased mechanical compliance ref [87]. In inertial devices, such variability can broaden focused streams or cause overlap with leukocyte trajectories, reducing purity despite acceptable recovery.

Device design therefore increasingly accounts for mechanics rather than diameter alone. High-aspect-ratio channels, Dean-coupled spirals, and multistage architectures can partially compensate by repeatedly reconditioning trajectories, but robust operation still depends on controlling sample preparation, flow rate, and hematocrit to limit mechanically induced dispersion. Recent reviews of CTC biophysics and liquid-biopsy technologies emphasize that integrating deformability with inertial migration models is essential for translating inertial enrichment from idealized cell lines to clinically heterogeneous patient samples ref [88], ref [89].

subsections.section_title: Centrifugal Microfluidic Systems and Lab-on-a-Disc Approaches
subsections.content:
Lab-on-a-disc (LoaD) platforms exploit rotation to convert motor control into programmable fluid handling. The dominant body force is centrifugal, which drives liquids radially outward with a pressure head that scales with angular velocity and radial position; this permits pumping without external syringes or pressure sources. Early work established how chamber geometry, rotational speed, and liquid volume jointly determine transfer, metering, and aliquoting behavior, making centrifugal microfluidics especially attractive for self-contained processing of clinical samples ref [90], ref [91].

In practice, LoaD actuation emerges from the interplay of centrifugal, capillary, viscous, and pneumatic effects. Rotation can sediment cells and particles according to density and size, while capillary barriers, hydrophobic patches, and trapped-air compression define burst thresholds and routing decisions. Comprehensive reviews have emphasized that this coupling enables serial unit operations—including mixing, valving, separation, and reagent release—using only controlled spin profiles and passive structures, thereby reducing system complexity relative to externally actuated microfluidics ref [37], ref [40].

For cancer cell processing, these principles are valuable because rare-cell enrichment often requires gentle, closed, and automation-compatible transport. Disc architectures can preload reagents, meter blood fractions, and synchronize density-based or filtration steps under reproducible rotational protocols. The broader centrifugal microfluidics literature has therefore framed LoaD as a scalable platform in which fluid actuation is encoded at the design stage and executed through time-varying rotation, supporting robust sample-to-answer workflows for bioanalytical and diagnostic applications ref [92], ref [93].

subsections.section_title: Centrifugal Microfluidic Systems and Lab-on-a-Disc Approaches
subsections.content:
Density-based and sedimentation-assisted separation on centrifugal platforms exploits the strong radial body force generated during disc rotation to stratify blood components and concentrate rare cells without external pumps. In this regime, particles or cells migrate according to their effective density, size, and deformability relative to the suspending medium, making the approach particularly compatible with whole-blood preprocessing. Early lab-on-a-disc demonstrations established that red blood cells and nucleated fractions can be differentially sedimented and retained in rotational chambers, enabling compact implementations of plasma extraction and cell fractionation ref [94], ref [95].

For cancer applications, these principles have been adapted to enrich circulating tumor cells (CTCs) by combining sedimentation with geometrically defined collection zones or density barriers. CTCs generally overlap hematologic cells in size and buoyant density, so centrifugal sedimentation alone rarely yields high-purity isolation; instead, it is most effective as a front-end depletion or concentration step that reduces sample volume and white-cell burden before finer discrimination. Systems such as fluid-assisted separation technology on discs have shown that carefully tuned rotational acceleration and deceleration can stabilize interfaces and improve recovery from minimally processed blood while maintaining clinically relevant throughput ref [96], ref [97].

A key advantage of sedimentation-based workflows is their low structural complexity relative to affinity capture modules, but performance is sensitive to hematocrit, chamber depth, and residence time. Consequently, recent centrifugal systems increasingly hybridize density-driven fractionation with membrane capture or downstream imaging to offset the intrinsic purity limits of sedimentation-only separation ref [98], ref [99].

subsections.section_title: Centrifugal Microfluidic Systems and Lab-on-a-Disc Approaches
subsections.content:
Centrifugal filtration extends lab-on-a-disc operation beyond density stratification by introducing size-selective retention under radially driven flow. In these systems, porous membranes, microfabricated weirs, or packed filtration layers are positioned so that increasing centrifugal pressure forces plasma or buffer through the barrier while larger particles or cells are retained upstream. Reviews of centrifugal microfluidics emphasize that such membrane-coupled unit operations are particularly attractive for whole-blood processing because they can be integrated with metering, sedimentation, and downstream analysis on the same rotating substrate ref [23], ref [100].

Membrane-integrated discs have been used extensively for blood plasma extraction, a closely related operation that illustrates both the utility and the constraints of centrifugal filtration. Czugala et al. demonstrated a laser-actuated disc in which membrane-based plasma separation was combined with automated reagent handling for colorimetric analysis, showing how rotationally generated transmembrane pressure can support clinically relevant sample preparation ref [101]. Similar design logic was advanced in fully integrated centrifugal platforms for biochemical assays, where membrane separation reduced manual preprocessing and enabled direct coupling to detection chambers ref [102]. These studies highlight key engineering trade-offs: pore size and membrane area determine throughput, whereas excessive pressure or prolonged spinning can promote clogging, hemolysis, or loss of rare target cells.

For cancer cell enrichment, membrane-based centrifugal modules are most useful when deployed either as prefilters to remove erythrocytes and debris or as gentle concentration stages after bulk sedimentation. The broader rare-cell literature has shown that filtration can recover circulating tumor cells on the basis of size and deformability, but performance is highly sensitive to membrane fouling and cell stress ref [7], ref [103]. Consequently, disc implementations increasingly combine filtration with timed valving and staged spin protocols so that membrane loading is distributed over time rather than imposed in a single high-shear step, an approach consistent with general centrifugal flow-control strategies summarized by Strohmeier et al. ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Centrifugal Microfluidic Systems and Lab-on-a-Disc Approaches
subsections.subsection_title: Valving, siphoning, and flow control elements
subsections.content:
Valving and flow-routing elements are central to lab-on-a-disc operation because centrifugal pumping is inherently global, whereas cancer sample preparation requires local, sequential control of metering, incubation, washing, and transfer. Early centrifugal microfluidic platforms established capillary and hydrophobic burst valves as rotationally addressable barriers whose opening threshold depends on channel geometry, surface energy, and spin rate, enabling programmable release of aliquots without external actuators ref [23], ref [104]. Such passive valves are attractive for rare-cell workflows because they minimize mechanical complexity while supporting parallelized unit operations on compact discs.

Siphon-based transfer elements further expand process logic by decoupling liquid displacement from instantaneous centrifugal pressure. Once primed, capillary siphons can move liquids from outer to inner radial positions during controlled speed changes, allowing timed reagent exchange, pellet resuspension, or supernatant removal after sedimentation. The integration of capillary priming structures and event-triggered siphons has been particularly influential in implementing multi-step assays and serial processing chains on rotating platforms ref [105], ref [106]. In cancer enrichment settings, these mechanisms help preserve fragile cells by avoiding abrupt pneumatic or mechanical actuation.

More advanced flow control has combined passive structures with externally triggered valves, including laser-actuated ferrowax microvalves and other switchable barriers that permit on-demand release independent of the current rotational state ref [107]. Reviews of centrifugal microfluidics have emphasized that robust disc performance depends on matching valve thresholds, siphon priming conditions, venting, and rotational protocols to the rheology and cellular content of clinical specimens ref [37]. Consequently, flow-control design is not merely an auxiliary engineering detail but a determinant of recovery, purity, and assay reproducibility in integrated lab-on-a-disc cancer workflows.

subsections.section_title: Centrifugal Microfluidic Systems and Lab-on-a-Disc Approaches
subsections.content:
Integrated sample-to-answer centrifugal workflows seek to collapse the full analytical chain—sample metering, plasma or buffy-coat preparation, target enrichment, reagent routing, amplification, and readout—onto a single rotating cartridge. In centrifugal formats, this integration is attractive because fluid transport can be programmed through spin rate, capillary barriers, siphons, and event-triggered valves without external pumps. Early demonstrations established that immunoassay processing and nucleic-acid analysis could be automated on compact disc-like platforms, defining the architectural basis for closed, clinically oriented disposable systems ref [108], ref [109].

For cancer-oriented use cases, the value of such workflows lies in minimizing manual transfers that otherwise compromise rare-cell recovery and molecular fidelity. Disc systems have therefore been coupled to upstream blood preparation and downstream molecular detection modules, including plasma extraction for circulating biomarkers and integrated lysis/amplification chambers for mutation analysis. Illustrative examples include centrifugal cartridges for automated plasma separation from whole blood ref [110], fully integrated microfluidic compact discs for nucleic acid analysis ref [111], and disc-based multiplex real-time PCR platforms that combine aliquoting, thermal processing, and optical detection ref [112].

Although many current lab-on-a-disc systems interrogate circulating nucleic acids rather than intact circulating tumor cells, the same sample-to-answer design logic is directly relevant to cancer cell workflows: enrichment modules must be synchronized with washing, staining, or lysis steps while preserving cell viability or analyte integrity. Recent integrated cartridges that combine extraction and isothermal amplification further show how sealed centrifugal processing can reduce contamination risk and operator dependence, an important consideration for decentralized oncology testing ref [113].

subsections.section_title: Centrifugal Microfluidic Systems and Lab-on-a-Disc Approaches
subsections.content:
Operational optimization in centrifugal microfluidic systems is governed by the coupling between spin rate, radial position, channel geometry, and fluid properties, all of which determine pressure generation, residence time, and the onset of valve or siphon actuation. A useful design strategy is to treat the disc as a sequence of rotationally programmed unit operations, so that acceleration, deceleration, and dwell periods are co-optimized with capillary thresholds and sedimentation kinetics rather than selected independently ref [23], ref [114]. This systems view is particularly important for rare-cell workflows, where excessive shear, unstable interfaces, or poorly timed transfer steps can degrade recovery and purity.

From an engineering perspective, optimization often centers on rotational protocols that stabilize priming and metering while minimizing dispersion and pellet disturbance. Event-triggered and pulse-actuated flow control schemes have shown that transient changes in angular velocity can improve the robustness of liquid routing compared with constant-speed operation ref [115], ref [116]. Similar considerations apply to centrifugo-pneumatic and dissolvable-film based architectures, where the timing of pneumatic compression, siphon activation, and reagent release must be matched to specimen viscosity and loaded volume to avoid premature valving failures or incomplete transfer ref [117], ref [118].

For cancer cell enrichment, these operational choices translate directly into analytical performance. Optimized spin profiles can enhance sedimentation-assisted preconcentration, reduce clogging in downstream filters, and improve reproducibility across patient-to-patient variations in hematocrit or debris burden. More broadly, the progression toward sample-to-answer discs has motivated quantitative design frameworks that combine burst-frequency prediction, capillary modeling, and workflow-level reliability analysis, enabling rotational systems to move from empirically tuned prototypes toward clinically robust platforms ref [23], ref [117], ref [119].

subsections.section_title: Performance Evaluation, Biomedical Translation, and Comparative Assessment
subsections.content:
Key performance metrics for inertial and centrifugal cancer-cell separation extend beyond simple capture rate. The most commonly reported quantities are recovery (fraction of target cells collected), purity (fraction of collected cells that are target cells), enrichment factor relative to the input composition, throughput or volumetric processing rate, and limit of detection for rare-cell contexts such as circulating tumor cells. Inertial microfluidic studies have emphasized the trade-off between high flow rate and separation fidelity, showing that channel geometry and particle-size contrast jointly determine recovery and purity at clinically relevant throughputs ref [34], ref [120]. Centrifugal platforms similarly report separation efficiency as a function of rotational speed, residence time, and density contrast, often prioritizing simple operation and parallel processing over maximal enrichment ref [121].

For cancer applications, analytical performance should also be interpreted with respect to heterogeneity in cell size, deformability, and clustering. Size-only metrics can overestimate performance when tumor cells overlap with leukocytes in diameter, a limitation highlighted in comparative studies of label-free CTC enrichment technologies ref [122]. Accordingly, reporting should include false-positive carryover, depletion of background blood cells, and performance on spiked versus patient-derived samples. Inertial approaches that rely on Dean-coupled focusing or vortex trapping often achieve very high throughput, but their apparent recovery can vary substantially with tumor-cell phenotype and operating point ref [123], ref [124].

A useful evaluation framework therefore combines engineering and biological endpoints: recovery, purity, enrichment, throughput, reproducibility, and coefficient of variation across runs, together with post-separation viability and molecular integrity. Standardized metric definitions remain essential because differences in counting method, spiking protocol, and denominator choice can make headline efficiencies difficult to compare across platforms ref [122], ref [125].

subsections.section_title: Performance Evaluation, Biomedical Translation, and Comparative Assessment
subsections.content:
Experimental validation of inertial and centrifugal cancer-cell separation platforms spans a progression from simplified model suspensions to clinically relevant blood matrices. Early studies commonly used cultured tumor cell lines spiked into buffer or diluted whole blood to quantify recovery, purity, and throughput under controlled size and deformability contrasts. For inertial systems, this strategy was central to demonstrating label-free enrichment of rare tumor cells from blood analogs and patient-like samples, while also enabling direct comparison with benchmark immunomagnetic approaches ref [18], ref [65].

A second tier of validation uses increasingly complex specimens, including lysed or minimally processed whole blood, peripheral blood from patients with metastatic disease, and occasionally pleural effusions or other liquid-biopsy-type samples. Inertial microfluidic technologies such as vortex and spiral devices have been tested on patient blood to confirm that performance observed in spike-in experiments does not fully translate linearly to native circulating tumor cell populations, which are more heterogeneous in size, phenotype, and cluster state ref [126], ref [127]. This distinction is especially important because clinically relevant targets may overlap biophysically with leukocytes or exist as multicellular aggregates.

For centrifugal systems, validation has similarly moved from bead and cell-line surrogates toward blood-based rare-cell isolation in rotating-disc formats, where hydrodynamic stability and ease of automation are attractive for point-of-care workflows ref [128]. Across both classes, rigorous experimental validation increasingly requires matched spike-in and patient cohorts, orthogonal molecular or immunocytochemical confirmation of captured cells, and reporting of pre-analytical variables such as anticoagulant, storage time, and blood dilution, all of which materially influence apparent separation performance ref [65], ref [129].

subsections.section_title: Performance Evaluation, Biomedical Translation, and Comparative Assessment
subsections.content:
For cancer cell separation, viability is not a peripheral metric but a prerequisite for downstream molecular and functional analyses. In both inertial and centrifugal platforms, the principal risks arise from hydrodynamic shear, extensional stress, repeated acceleration–deceleration, and prolonged residence in nonphysiological buffers. Studies on spiral and contraction–expansion inertial devices have generally reported high post-processing viability when flow conditions are tuned below damaging stress regimes, while preserving recoveries suitable for subsequent culture or staining workflows ref [130], ref [131]. More broadly, the need to preserve intact, label-free circulating tumor cells (CTCs) has been emphasized by size-based microfluidic enrichment studies that couple enumeration with cytopathology or molecular profiling ref [7].

Downstream compatibility is best judged by whether isolated cells remain usable for immunocytochemistry, fluorescence in situ hybridization, nucleic-acid analysis, and ex vivo culture. The CTC-iChip exemplified this translational benchmark by enabling negative-depletion-based enrichment with compatibility for imaging and molecular characterization of rare tumor cells ref [132]. Similarly, cluster-preserving microfluidic approaches demonstrated that gentle handling can retain multicellular aggregates and support transcriptomic and biological interrogation, underscoring that mechanical integrity matters alongside simple live/dead readouts ref [133]. In centrifugal systems, acceptable viability is achievable, but hemolysis, leukocyte activation, and pellet compaction become practical concerns when high g-forces or long spin times are used, particularly for fragile CTCs.

Accordingly, reporting standards should move beyond immediate viability percentages to include apoptosis markers, short-term proliferation, RNA quality, and assay-specific success rates after separation. This is especially important because epithelial and mesenchymal tumor cells differ in deformability and stress tolerance, so a device optimized for recovery may still bias downstream biology by selectively damaging vulnerable subpopulations ref [134]. Pragmatically, the most clinically relevant systems are those that maintain cellular integrity across the entire workflow—from blood processing to fixation, culture, or sequencing—rather than maximizing enrichment alone ref [7], ref [132], ref [134].

subsections.section_title: Performance Evaluation, Biomedical Translation, and Comparative Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Comparative analysis of inertial versus centrifugal systems
subsections.content:
Inertial and centrifugal microfluidic systems exploit different force balances and therefore occupy complementary regions of the cancer-cell-separation design space. Inertial devices use shear-gradient and wall-induced lift, often augmented by Dean drag in curved channels, to achieve high-throughput, sheathless size-based focusing with relatively simple continuous-flow operation; this makes them attractive for rapid processing of diluted blood and for integration with upstream/downstream microfluidic modules ref [135], ref [29]. By contrast, centrifugal systems generate body forces through rotation, enabling pumping, valving, mixing, and sedimentation or density-stratified separation on a single disc platform without external syringe pumps, which is advantageous for compact and potentially user-friendly workflows ref [37], ref [136].

From an analytical perspective, inertial approaches have generally demonstrated higher volumetric throughput and easier parallelization, but they are more sensitive to channel geometry, particle concentration, and hematocrit-dependent hydrodynamics, which can complicate performance consistency in whole blood ref [135], ref [31]. Centrifugal systems can handle more heterogeneous samples and support multistep on-disc preprocessing, yet separation resolution may depend strongly on rotational protocol, density contrast, and sedimentation time, sometimes limiting recovery of rare circulating tumor cells unless combined with immunocapture or other enrichment steps ref [37], ref [136]. Thus, inertial platforms tend to favor label-free, morphology-driven enrichment, whereas centrifugal platforms more readily support workflow automation and sample-to-answer integration.

For translational use, the trade-off is often between throughput and operational self-containment. Reviews of inertial microfluidics emphasize manufacturable channel architectures but also note the challenge of standardizing cutoffs across cancer types with overlapping size and deformability distributions ref [29]. Disc-based centrifugal microfluidics has progressed toward robust unit operations and portable instrumentation, although balancing mechanical complexity, cartridge cost, and assay reproducibility remains central to clinical deployment ref [136], ref [23]. Comparative benchmarking should therefore evaluate not only recovery and purity, but also preprocessing burden, clogging tolerance, automation level, and compatibility with molecular downstream analyses.

subsections.section_title: Performance Evaluation, Biomedical Translation, and Comparative Assessment
subsections.content:
Manufacturability is a major discriminator between high-performing laboratory prototypes and clinically deployable separators. In inertial microfluidics, translational potential is strengthened by simple planar geometries, passive operation, and compatibility with high-throughput replication methods such as injection molding or hot embossing, particularly for spiral and contraction–expansion architectures ref [137], ref [138]. By contrast, more elaborate three-dimensional channel networks or designs that require tightly controlled sheath flows can complicate packaging, alignment, and quality control at scale. For centrifugal platforms, manufacturability benefits from disc-based formats that integrate pumping and valving through rotation, but practical deployment depends on robust cartridge sealing, balance control, and reproducible fabrication of multilayer polymer assemblies ref [23], ref [49].

System integration also determines whether separation can be embedded into realistic cancer liquid-biopsy workflows. Several groups have shown that inertial systems can be coupled upstream to bulk blood handling and downstream to imaging or molecular analysis, including label-free CTC enrichment in integrated microfluidic devices ref [139], ref [140]. Centrifugal systems are attractive for point-of-care settings because fluid actuation, metering, and multiplexing can be consolidated on a single spinning cartridge, reducing external peripherals ref [23], ref [49]. However, both approaches still face common engineering bottlenecks: clog-resistant operation with whole blood, bubble management, sterile single-use consumables, and interfaces to standardized collection tubes and analytical readouts.

From a commercialization perspective, integration must be assessed together with regulatory and operational constraints rather than separation physics alone. Designs that minimize user steps, eliminate external pumps, tolerate manufacturing variation, and preserve compatibility with cytology or sequencing are more likely to progress beyond proof-of-concept. This helps explain continued interest in passive inertial chips for front-end enrichment and in centrifugal cartridge systems for sample-to-answer automation, even when absolute analytical performance is similar.

subsections.section_title: Performance Evaluation, Biomedical Translation, and Comparative Assessment
subsections.content:
A persistent obstacle in evaluating inertial and centrifugal cancer-cell separation platforms is the absence of standardized benchmark materials, operating protocols, and reporting conventions. Reported recovery, purity, enrichment, and throughput often depend strongly on whether studies use cultured cell lines, fixed cells, bead surrogates, or patient-derived specimens, making cross-study comparison unreliable. This problem is amplified in circulating tumor cell (CTC) research, where pre-analytical variation in blood collection, storage, anticoagulants, and processing time can dominate device-level effects ref [141], ref [142]. Even established assay frameworks have highlighted substantial inter-laboratory variability when rare-cell measurements are not tightly controlled ref [143].

Benchmarking is further complicated by the fact that size-based and inertia- or centrifugation-driven devices are sensitive to hematocrit, leukocyte background, cell deformability, and aggregate formation, yet these variables are not reported consistently. Reviews of microfluidic CTC technologies have therefore emphasized the need for common performance definitions, standardized spike-in concentrations, and testing across clinically relevant concentration ranges rather than idealized model systems ref [144], ref [145]. For translational assessment, analytical recovery should be paired with orthogonal readouts such as post-sort viability, molecular integrity, and concordance with accepted clinical comparators.

A practical path forward is to adopt shared reference samples, blinded multi-site studies, and minimum reporting checklists that include sample provenance, processing delay, flow conditions, replicate structure, and uncertainty estimates. Broader standards initiatives in microfluidics and liquid biopsy suggest that reproducibility and interoperability improve when device claims are evaluated against consensus protocols rather than laboratory-specific optimizations ref [146], ref [147]. Such benchmarking will be essential for determining whether apparent differences between inertial and centrifugal systems reflect true technological advantages or simply nonuniform test conditions.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Hybrid Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
Hybrid inertial-centrifugal systems are emerging as a pragmatic route to extend the operating window of label-free cancer cell separation beyond what either mechanism can achieve alone. Inertial focusing provides high-throughput ordering and size-dependent lateral migration in straight or curved microchannels, while centrifugal actuation supplies compact, pump-free flow generation and tunable body forces suitable for point-of-care formats. Foundational inertial studies established how lift forces and Dean-coupled migration can continuously enrich larger and less deformable cells from blood at clinically relevant throughputs, creating a natural front end for subsequent centrifugal fractionation or concentration stages ref [34], ref [148].

Recent multimodal implementations increasingly combine these physical principles with secondary selection modules to improve purity and preserve rare-cell recovery. On centrifugal microfluidic platforms, sedimentation- and filtration-based workflows have already shown the feasibility of automating circulating tumor cell (CTC) enrichment from whole blood in rotating cartridges, suggesting a compatible architecture for integrating inertial prefocusing upstream of capture or wash steps ref [149], ref [150]. More broadly, multimodal chip designs that merge hydrodynamic sorting with deterministic displacement, microfiltration, or affinity interfaces can compensate for the limited specificity of purely biophysical separation, especially for overlapping leukocyte-CTC size distributions and fragile CTC clusters ref [151], ref [152].

The main design challenge is not simply stacking modules, but matching force scales, residence times, and shear histories across them. Future hybrid inertial-centrifugal devices will likely rely on sequential coarse-to-fine processing: inertial ordering for debulking, centrifugal concentration for volumetric reduction, and a final orthogonal stage for high-purity isolation or analysis. Such architectures are attractive for translational systems because they can reduce external peripherals while maintaining continuous operation, but their success will depend on robust handling of sample variability, clog resistance, and standardized recovery metrics across heterogeneous rare-cell phenotypes ref [152], ref [153].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Hybrid Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Coupling with affinity-based and biosensing modules
subsections.content:
A major trend in inertial and centrifugal microfluidics is the integration of label-free enrichment with downstream affinity capture to balance throughput and specificity. In this architecture, hydrodynamic forces first deplete erythrocytes and most leukocytes, thereby reducing the burden on antibody-functionalized regions that target EpCAM, HER2, EGFR, or other surface markers. Such hybrid workflows are motivated by the high-throughput, size-based focusing of inertial systems and by the established analytical performance of immunocapture platforms for circulating tumor cells (CTCs) ref [154], ref [7]. They are particularly attractive for low-abundance samples, where a pre-enrichment stage can improve effective target concentration while lowering nonspecific adhesion and reagent consumption.

The same logic extends to biosensing modules placed after physical separation. Once rare cells are concentrated into narrower streams or smaller collection volumes, electrochemical, optical, or impedance-based sensors can interrogate captured cells with improved signal-to-background ratio. Early demonstrations of integrated CTC chips showed that capture surfaces can be combined with on-chip staining and imaging for molecular characterization ref [155], while micro-Hall detection illustrated how affinity labeling can be merged with compact magnetic biosensing for rapid profiling of tumor cells in blood ref [156]. More recently, centrifugal disc formats have coupled immunomagnetic operations and automated sample handling, highlighting a route toward sample-to-answer processing in clinically practical cartridges ref [157].

A key challenge for affinity-coupled systems is biological heterogeneity: epithelial-marker dependence can miss cells undergoing epithelial-mesenchymal transition or traveling as clusters. This has motivated multimarker cocktails, reversible capture chemistries, and post-enrichment biosensing strategies that assay secreted proteins or genomic content rather than relying solely on one surface antigen ref [158], ref [159]. Future designs will likely combine inertial or centrifugal preprocessing with multiplexed capture and real-time sensing, enabling adaptive workflows that preserve viability while expanding phenotypic coverage.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Hybrid Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
Computational modeling has become central to the rational design of inertial and centrifugal microfluidic separators, replacing largely empirical channel tuning with predictive maps of lift, Dean drag, and particle migration equilibria. Foundational analyses of inertial migration in Poiseuille flow and curved microchannels clarified how confinement, Reynolds number, and secondary flows jointly determine focusing positions and throughput limits, providing a basis for geometry selection in spiral, contraction–expansion, and multiplexed devices ref [160], ref [161], ref [34]. For centrifugal platforms, numerical treatment of coupled Coriolis, centrifugal, and viscous effects is increasingly important because rotation-induced body forces can shift operating windows and interact nonlinearly with size- and deformability-dependent trajectories.

Recent work is moving from forward simulation to data-driven optimization. High-fidelity CFD and particle tracing can now be coupled with surrogate models or design-of-experiments frameworks to explore large parameter spaces more efficiently than exhaustive prototyping. This trend is especially relevant for cancer cell separation, where subtle differences in size, shape, and mechanical phenotype between circulating tumor cells and leukocytes demand robust optimization under biological variability. Reviews of inertial microfluidics have emphasized the need for integrated modeling across fluid mechanics, cell biomechanics, and device architecture, while translational studies have shown that throughput, recovery, and purity must be co-optimized rather than treated independently ref [29], ref [162].

A key future direction is closed-loop optimization that combines simulations, on-chip imaging, and machine-learning classifiers to adapt operating conditions in real time. Such frameworks could help compensate for patient-to-patient heterogeneity, improve cluster-preserving operation, and quantify uncertainty for regulatory validation. More broadly, physically informed learning strategies appear well suited to bridge the gap between idealized particle models and clinically relevant rare-cell suspensions containing deformable single cells, aggregates, and blood-cell background ref [29], ref [163].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Hybrid Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
A central challenge for inertial and centrifugal microfluidic cancer cell separation is that rare circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are not a uniform target population. CTCs span epithelial, mesenchymal, stem-like, apoptotic, and hybrid phenotypic states, and these transitions alter cell size, deformability, and surface-marker expression, thereby reshaping device recovery and purity. Clinical and biological studies have shown substantial inter- and intra-patient heterogeneity, including the presence of epithelial–mesenchymal transition programs that can undermine purely marker-based enrichment and motivate label-free or multimodal strategies ref [164], ref [165].

Cluster isolation further raises the stakes because multicellular CTC aggregates appear to possess disproportionately high metastatic potential while being mechanically fragile and rare. Aceto et al. demonstrated that CTC clusters are oligoclonal precursors of breast cancer metastasis, while Sarioglu et al. introduced a microfluidic approach specifically designed to preserve and isolate clusters by exploiting asymmetric flow and size-dependent behavior rather than harsh filtration ref [158], ref [166]. These observations suggest that future inertial-centrifugal platforms should be tuned not only for single-cell focusing windows but also for low-shear handling, wider operational tolerances, and architecture-aware collection of large aggregates.

An additional design implication is the need to resolve biologically meaningful subpopulations after enrichment. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling has revealed distinct CTC lineages and expression programs linked to therapy resistance and disease progression, underscoring the value of downstream molecular compatibility ref [167]. In parallel, physical studies indicate that cluster-specific vulnerabilities, such as junctional dependencies, may be therapeutically actionable ref [168]. Thus, next-generation rare-cell workflows should prioritize recovery of viable singles and clusters across a broad phenotypic spectrum, while minimizing bias introduced by size cutoffs, deformability thresholds, or antigen selection.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Hybrid Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
Clinical translation of inertial and centrifugal microfluidic cancer cell separation depends less on proof-of-principle capture alone than on analytical validity under clinically realistic conditions. For circulating tumor cell (CTC) applications, this means reproducible recovery across low-abundance samples, preservation of cell integrity for downstream molecular assays, and robust operation with heterogeneous blood matrices. Experience from clinically deployed CellSearch studies established the importance of standardized pre-analytical handling, operator-independent workflows, and clearly defined performance metrics for rare-cell assays ref [1], ref [2]. Similar expectations now apply to label-free microfluidic platforms, which must demonstrate not only enrichment efficiency but also inter-site reproducibility and clinical concordance with accepted reference methods.

Regulatory considerations are shaped by intended use. Devices positioned as sample-preparation tools for research face lower barriers than in vitro diagnostic systems that directly inform treatment decisions. Translation therefore requires design controls, risk management, and manufacturing consistency compatible with quality-system requirements, alongside evidence for precision, linearity, limit of detection, and interference testing. Broader liquid-biopsy guidance also underscores the need for fit-for-purpose validation, especially when CTC isolation is coupled to genomic or phenotypic readouts that may alter patient stratification ref [169], ref [170]. For inertial-centrifugal hybrids, additional attention is needed for sterility, closed-cartridge integration, hemocompatibility, and mitigation of clogging or cross-contamination during high-throughput processing.

A further challenge is clinical utility: enriched rare cells must yield information that changes management, not merely demonstrate technical feasibility. Studies linking CTC enumeration to prognosis in metastatic breast, prostate, and colorectal cancer helped define this translational benchmark ref [2], while more recent position papers emphasize that biomarker assays require evidence frameworks spanning analytical validity, clinical validity, and utility ref [171], ref [172]. Accordingly, future success of inertial and centrifugal systems will likely depend on multicenter prospective studies, harmonized reporting standards, and early regulatory co-development of integrated hardware-software workflows.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Hybrid Strategies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
Despite major progress, several open problems continue to limit inertial and centrifugal microfluidic cancer-cell separation. A central challenge is the mismatch between idealized model systems and the biophysical diversity of clinical specimens: circulating tumor cells (CTCs) span broad ranges of size, deformability, epithelial–mesenchymal state, and cluster architecture, so size- or inertia-dominant designs inevitably risk missing clinically relevant subpopulations ref [158], ref [173]. This problem is compounded by the rarity of target cells and by sample-dependent effects from hematocrit, coagulation, and leukocyte activation, which can perturb focusing behavior and reduce reproducibility.

Future opportunities therefore lie in adaptive and multimodal platforms that combine passive hydrodynamics with deformability-, affinity-, or imaging-based discrimination while preserving viability for downstream molecular analysis. Particular emphasis should be placed on robust isolation of CTC clusters, whose metastatic significance is disproportionate to their abundance, yet whose fragility makes them difficult to recover in high yield ref [174], ref [175]. Integrating label-free enrichment with single-cell and cluster-resolved omics could also help reconcile device outputs with tumor evolution and treatment resistance.

A second frontier is standardization and translation. Benchmarking across platforms remains inconsistent with respect to recovery, purity, throughput, and preanalytical handling, making cross-study comparison difficult ref [176]. More predictive computational frameworks that couple particle migration, cell mechanics, and clinically realistic suspension properties may support data-driven design, but they must be validated on multicenter patient cohorts. Ultimately, clinically deployable systems will require manufacturable cartridges, closed-loop automation, and evidence that CTC enumeration or characterization adds value beyond established liquid-biopsy assays such as circulating tumor DNA ref [177].
